abstract: Renal ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) is an important cause of acute kidney injury (AKI). However, the pathophysiological changes and mechanisms during IRI-AKI progression remain unclear. This study aims toinvestigate the potential mechanisms in the progression of IRI-AKI by integrating metabolomics and transcriptomics data, providing a reference for the subsequent identification of biomarkers and therapeutic targets. IRI-AKI rat models with 30 min of ischemia and 24–72 h of reperfusion surgery simulating the progression of AKI were established. Compared to the control group underwent sham surgery (NC group), most of the differentially expressed metabolites (DEMs) in IRI-AKI 24 h and IRI-AKI 72 h decreased, mainly including amino acids, organic acids, and carnitines. Additionally, we found that DEMs were mainly enriched in amino acid-related pathways, among which valine, leucine, and isoleucine biosynthesis were dramatically altered in all comparisons. Transcriptomics revealed that differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were primarily involved in amino acid, lipid, and fatty acid metabolism. By integrating metabolomics and transcriptomics, we found valine, leucine, and isoleucine biosynthesis play key roles in IRI-AKI development. Our findings concluded that valine, leucine, and isoleucine pathways are hubs that potentially connect transcriptomes to metabolomes, providing new insights regarding the pathogenesis of IRI-AKI and its potential biomarkers and therapeutic strategies. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1038/s41598-024-81600-x.

Materials and methods
IRI-AKI models and sample collection
Eighteen male Sprague-Dawley rats (age, 7–8 weeks; weight, 220–250 g) were procured from Bainte Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Hubei, China) and acclimatized for a period of one week. The rats were provided with a standard commercially available pelleted diet and tap water ad libitum. All animals were individually housed in metabolic cages equipped with urine and feces separators. As previously reported, 12 rats were subjected to bilateral renal IRI by clamping the renal pedicle for 30 min at 37 °C
21
,
22
. After removing the clamps, the restoration of blood flow in the kidneys was verified to preliminarily assess the success of the AKI models. Rats in the experimental group were euthanized under isoflurane anesthesia at 24 h (24 h group,
n
= 6) or 72 h (72 h group,
n
= 6) postoperatively. The study selected the 24 h and 72 h reperfusion time points for investigating the pathogenesis of IRI-AKI because preliminary experiments showed that kidney function indicators (UREA, BUN and CREA) measured at four reperfusion times (8 h, 24 h, 48 h and 72 h) exhibited a progressive increase. Based on these findings, we chose the 24 h point (where kidney function abnormalities were first observed) and the 72 h point (where the indicators were most severe) for formal study (Figure
S1
).
Control animals underwent sham surgery and were euthanized under isoflurane anesthesia at 72 h postoperatively (normal control [NC] group,
n
= 6). Heparinized blood samples were centrifuged at 13,000×
g
for 10 min at 4 °C to obtain plasma for biochemical analysis. The right kidney was frozen in liquid nitrogen for the omics analysis, and the left kidney was fixed in 10% neutral-buffered formalin for the histopathological analysis
22
.
Animals ethics statement
All animal experiments and procedures were conducted in strict accordance with the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals of the National Institutes of Health and reported in accordance with ARRIVE guidelines. The ethical committee of Bainte Biotechnology Co., Ltd. approved all experimental procedures (statement number IACUC-BNB-2024-003).
Biochemical and histopathological examinations
Plasma creatinine (CREA), urea, and blood urea nitrogen levels were measured using an enzymatic method with Rayto reagents and a Chemray 380 biochemistry analyzer. Kidney biopsy specimens were processed using conventional methods to prepare paraffin and ultrathin electron microscopy sections as previously described
23
. Sagittal sections (5 μm) of the kidney were examined after hematoxylin and eosin and TdT-mediated dUTP nick-end labeling (TUNEL) staining to evaluate renal histopathological changes and detect renal tissue cell apoptosis using light microscopy. Transmission electron microscopy has a particularly crucial position in the pathological diagnosis of renal diseases because it enables the observation of the renal ultrastructure.
Ultraperformance liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry-based targeted metabolomics profiling
Kidney sample extraction and derivatization
Approximately 10 mg of each kidney sample was placed in a safe-lock tube, homogenized with 20 µL of Millipore ultrapure water, and extracted using 150 µL of cold methanol with the internal standard mix. After another 3 min of homogenization, the sample was centrifuged at 13,500×
g
at 4 °C for 10 min, and a 30 µL aliquot of the supernatant was carefully transferred to a 96-well plate for derivatization
24
,
25
. A 10 µL aliquot of freshly prepared derivative reagents (200 mM 3-NPH in 75% aqueous methanol and 96 mM EDC-6% pyridine solution in methanol) was added to each well, and the plate was sealed for 60 min of derivatization at 30 °C
24
. Subsequently, the sample was evaporated for 2 h and reconstituted with 330 µL of 50% methanol solution
24
,
25
. Similar sample preparation methods were used for the quality control samples, which were prepared by mixing aliquots of the study samples to broadly represent the biological average of the entire sample set.
Metabolomics analysis
Targeted metabolites were detected using a Q300 Metabolite Array kit (Metabo Profile, Shanghai, China)
24
. The kit contained a comprehensive panel of 324 compounds from various chemical classes, including bile acids, amino acids, fatty acids, carboxylic acids, hydroxyl acids, phenolic acids, indoles, and others. These compounds were used as working standard solutions for calibration purposes to enable accurate quantification of metabolites in the samples and generate standard curve information on the metabolites of interest. Raw data files generated through ultraperformance liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry were processed using TMBQ software (version 1.0; HMI, Shenzhen, China) to perform peak integration, calibration, and quantitation. Calibrators were prepared for accurate quantification, including a blank sample (matrix sample processed without internal standard), a zero sample (matrix sample processed with internal standard), and a series of seven concentrations covering the expected range for the metabolites present in the specific biological samples (Table
S1
). iMAP (version 1.0; Metabo Profile, Shanghai, China) was used to perform a principal component analysis (PCA), orthogonal partial least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA), and pathway analysis. Finally, significantly differentially expressed metabolites (DEMs) that met the following criteria were included: Variable importance in projection (VIP) > 1; |log2 fold-change| (|log2FC|) > 0.585; and
P
< 0.05
26
,
27
.
RNA extraction and transcriptomic analysis
Rat kidney samples
Total RNA was extracted from kidney samples using TRIzol (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA), and the concentration, quality, and integrity were determined (NanoDrop; Thermo Fisher Scientific)
28
. Total RNA was selected for library construction using the NEBNext Ultra II RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (New England Biolabs Inc., Ipswich, MA, USA), which is a strand-specific library preparation kit. The selection of 400- to 500-bp complementary DNA fragments was performed using AMPure XP beads before polymerase chain reaction amplification was performed. Multiplexed DNA libraries were pooled in equal volumes after normalization. The pooled library was quantified, diluted, and sequenced on Illumina sequencers using the PE150 mode
29
.
Transcriptomics
Raw sequencing data were filtered to obtain clean data that were aligned to the reference genome. The expression of each gene was calculated, and aligned reads were assembled to reconstruct transcript sequences. HTSeq (version 0.9.1) was used to count the reads mapped to each gene (raw expression level). Expression levels were normalized to fragments per kilobase of transcript per million fragments. DESeq software (version 1.20.0) was used to compare differential expressions, and genes with a false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05 and |log2FC| >1 were considered DEGs
30
,
31
.
Integrating metabolomics and transcriptomics
Pearson’s correlation analysis of DEMs and DEGs was performed. Genes and metabolites with correlation coefficients (R) > 0.8 and
P
< 0.05 were selected for subsequent analyses. A clustering heatmap was generated to visually depict correlations and provide a visual representation of the relationships between genes and metabolites, thereby highlighting the correlation strength
32
.
Statistical analysis
Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, version 25.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Normally distributed data are presented as the mean ± standard deviation. A one-way analysis of variance was used to compare differences between multiple groups; in the case of variance heterogeneity, Welch’s approximate analysis of variance was applied, followed by Dunnett’s T3 test. During cross-sectional studies, Mann–Whitney’s U test, Wilcoxon’s rank-sum test, or Student’s t-test (two-tailed) was performed. Statistical significance was set at a threshold of
P
< 0.05.
Unsupervised non-targeted methods were used for the raw ultraperformance liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry data obtained through the PCA to visualize metabolomic variation. The OPLS-DA with supervised classification methods and unit variance scaling were used to maximize the identification of differential metabolites between groups, and key variables were determined using VIP scores
32
. Permutation testing of 200 random variables was performed to prevent overfitting of the OPLS-DA model.
A Gene Ontology (GO) analysis was performed using topGO, and FDRs were calculated using hypergeometric distribution (significant enrichment, FDR < 0.05). A Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analysis was performed using ClusterProfiler software (version 3.4.4) (significantly enriched pathways, FDR < 0.05)
33
,
34
.
Data records
Transcriptome sequencing was completed on the Illumina Hiseq 6000 platform, with a library size of 380 bp. The raw data has been submitted to the NCBI SRA database under accession code: PRJNA1159485 (
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/bioproject/PRJNA1159485
).
The raw LC-MS/MS data files were deposited at the MetaboLights database of the European Bioinformatics Institute under accession number: MTBLS11068 (
https://www.ebi.ac.uk/metabolights/editor/MTBLS11068/descriptors
).

Introduction
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common critical condition characterized by a rapid decline in kidney function within 48 h caused by structural or functional kidney damage
1
. Its clinical features include rapid progression, difficult early diagnosis, and high mortality rates
2
. AKI treatment mainly comprises symptomatic and supportive therapy as well as renal replacement therapy; however, the treatment effects are limited
3
. Ischemia–reperfusion injury (IRI) is a common cause of AKI that contributes to perioperative AKI incidence and mortality. Renal ischemia–reperfusion triggers events that induce oxidative stress, cellular dysfunction, and renal impairment
4
. However, there are gaps in our understanding of the precise molecular mechanisms involved in IRI-induced AKI (IRI-AKI). Particularly, the pathophysiological changes and mechanisms in the progression of IRI-AKI remain highly unclear.
Multiomics analyses, such as those involving metabolomics and transcriptomics, are increasingly being used to identify biomarkers and pathogenetic factors and mechanisms
5
,
6
. Metabolomics is the comprehensive analysis of small-molecule metabolites, and it is increasingly being applied to determine biomarkers and gain insights into biological processes and molecular mechanisms. Transcriptomics can be used to investigate and analyze transcript/messenger RNA expression, which can help identify biomarkers and molecular mechanisms. Directly associating transcriptomics with phenotypes is challenging; however, metabolomics can complement this association. The integration of transcriptomics and metabolomics enables the identification of key factors associated with metabolism and phenotypes, providing new insights regarding the pathogenesis of disease, its biomarkers, and therapeutic strategies
7
.
The kidney is associated with metabolic homeostasis and cellular metabolism
2
,
6
. There is a close association between kidney disease and metabolic abnormalities
8
. However, current research has primarily focused on metabolic disorders of chronic kidney disease, including abnormalities in glucose, amino acid, and lipid metabolism
9
–
11
. Metabolomic studies of AKI were limited and mainly focused on pediatric populations
12
–
14
and rat models induced by cisplatin
15
, rhabdomyolysis
16
, and sepsis
17
. Furthermore, there have been few systematic studies regarding changes in metabolic profiles associated with IRI-AKI and recovery. Some transcriptomics studies have linked renal injury in IRI-AKI models to differentially expressed genes (DEGs)
18
–
20
. Unfortunately, no studies have integrated metabolomics and transcriptomics to assess the molecular mechanisms underlying IRI-AKI.
Therefore, this study aimed to comprehensively analyze renal metabolic and transcriptional profiles associated with IRIinduced AKI rat models, explore the metabolic/genetic changes and mechanisms underlying IRI-AKI progression, providing diagnostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

Results
Establishment of the IRI-AKI model
Compared with the NC rats, IRI-AKI rats had elevated plasma CREA, urea, and blood urea nitrogen levels, preliminary indicating the model was successfully established (Fig.
1
A). Prolonged IRI exhibited significantly increased CREA, urea, and blood urea nitrogen plasma concentrations (Fig.
1
B). In the 24 h group, inflammatory cell infiltration and interstitial fibrosis were notably increased. The glomeruli exhibited predominantly normal histology or only mild pathological changes; however, in certain renal tubules, luminal dilation, loss of the brush border, and shedding of tubular epithelial cells were observed (Fig.
1
C. a & b). Epithelial cell shedding in the renal tubules was more pronounced in the 72 h group than in the 24 h group, and it was accompanied by vacuolar degeneration and the formation of a bare tubular basement membrane, which was indicative of acute tubular necrosis (Fig.
1
C. c & d). TUNEL staining indicated more apoptosis in the IRI-AKI rats than in the NC rats, and the degree of apoptosis was more pronounced with prolonged IRI (Fig.
1
C). Transmission electron microscopy revealed that podocytes in the NC group exhibited intact foot processes with clear structural organization. In the IRI-AKI group, podocytes displayed extensive fusion within foot processes characterized by evident vacuolization and necrosis (Fig.
1
C. e). Mitochondrial swelling, rupture, loss of mitochondrial structure, and nuclear condensation were observed (Fig.
1
C f & g). These results suggest that renal function deteriorated further with the prolongation of ischemic reinfusion time.
Fig. 1
Effects of acute kidney injury (AKI) induced by ischemia–reperfusion injury (IRI) on renal histological and functional indices. (
A
) Schematic of ischemic reperfusion and sample collection protocol. (
B
) Plasma levels of urea, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and creatinine (CREA). *

, ***

. (
C
) Renal tissue stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and TdT-mediated dUTP nick-end labeling (TUNEL). The transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis showed that IRI induced foot processes and mitochondria damage. Scale bar = 20 μm; ×40 magnification.
Metabolic profile
PCA scores indicated that quality control samples were closely clustered and demonstrated good instrument stability and data reproducibility (Fig.
2
A). Renal metabolite distributions among the three groups were effectively separated in the PCA score plot, and the PLS-DA further facilitated the effective separation of the renal metabolite distributions among the three groups (Fig.
2
A). When distinguishing metabolic differences using pairwise group comparisons, OPLS-DA demonstrated significant separation. To avoid overfitting the OPLS-DA model, a permutation test was performed by randomly shuffling the sample grouping 1000 times. The closer R2X, R2Y, and Q2 are to 1, the model is more stable and reliable. A model can be considered effective if Q2 is greater than 0.5, and outstanding if Q2 is greater than 0.9. Our results showed the R2Y were 0.971, 0.949, and 0.932, and Q2 were 0.697, 0.806 and 0.503 respectively in NC vs. IRI-AKI 24 h group, NC vs. IRI-AKI 72 h group and IRI-AKI 24 h vs. IRI-AKI 72 h group, indicating that the models were not overfit and could be further used Fig.
2
B). Based on the OPLS-DA of the model, significant DEMs were selected (criteria: VIP > 1,
P
< 0.05, and |log2FC| > 0.585). These DEMs were mainly amino acids, bile acids, carnitines, nucleotides and their analogs, fatty acids, organic acids and their derivatives, and benzoic acid derivatives.
Fig. 2
Statistical comparison of metabolites, analysis of differential metabolites, and key metabolic pathways. (
A
) Principal component analysis (PCA) and partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) score plots of comparisons of quality control (QC) of the normal control (NC) group, ischemia–reperfusion injury (IRI)-induced acute kidney injury (AKI) at 24 h (IRI-AKI 24 h) group, and IRI-AKI at 72 h (IRI-AKI 72 h) group. (
B
) Plots of orthogonal partial least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) scores and permutation test results. (
C
) Volcano plot of differentially expressed metabolites (DEMs) (NC vs. IRI-AKI 24 h; NC vs. IRI-AKI 72 h; and NC vs. IRI-AKI 24 h vs. IRI-AKI 72 h groups). (
D
) Heatmap of the top 25 different metabolites in the kidney. Upregulated and downregulated metabolites are shown in red and blue, respectively. (
E
) Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway of DEMs. Each circle represents a KEGG pathway, with annotations next to the circle indicating the pathway name. The x-axis represents the enrichment impact. A larger enrichment impact indicates a higher degree of enrichment. The color of the circle represents the P-values. Redder circles indicate smaller P-values and more reliable enrichment significance. The size of the circle reflects the number of enriched DEMs in the pathway, with a larger circle indicating a more significant enrichment of DEMs.
Volcano plots revealed 90 significant DEMs (9 upregulated and 81 downregulated) and 40 significant DEMs (7 upregulated and 33 downregulated) in IRI-AKI 24 h group and IRI-AKI 72 h group respectively compared to NC group (Fig.
2
C). The 24 h and 72 h groups consistently had 23 common significant DEMs (2 upregulated and 21 downregulated) (Table
1
and Figure
S2
). Most of the related metabolites in the IRI-AKI groups were decreased. Compared to the 24 h group, the 72 h group exhibited 6 DEMs, which were all upregulated, including one amino acid (dimethylglycine) and five organic acids (3-methyl-2-oxopentanoic acid, alpha-hydroxyisobutyric acid, ketoleucine, alpha-ketoisovaleric acid, and hydroxypropionic acid) (Table
S2
). To explore changes in DEMs during IRI-AKI development and identify potential early biomarkers, we performed a heatmap analysis of the top 25 DEMs in the kidney. These were mainly metabolites of amino acids, fatty acids, carnitine, bile acids, and carbohydrate. Notably, the top 25 DEMs in the 24 h and 72 h groups were not the same (Fig.
2
D). Moreover, citric and aconitic acids only exhibited higher expression in the 24 h group than they did in the NC group
35
,
36
.

Discussion
Research on AKI has primarily focused on sepsis-induced AKI models; however, most clinical AKI cases are associated with IRI. IRI is the pathological process by which ischemic tissues regain their blood supply, leading to tissue damage
40
. In most cases, renal IRI is reversible. Therefore, early detection and timely intervention are clinically significant for minimizing kidney damage and preserving renal function
40
,
41
. However, the pathophysiology of IRI-AKI is extremely complex and not fully understood. In this study, we combined metabolomics and transcriptomics to comprehensively understand the pathophysiological processes of IRI-AKI progression from the perspective of global gene expression and metabolite accumulation. This study aimed to identify the key genes and metabolites involved in IRI-AKI pathogenesis.
In this study, we demonstrated that certain substances, such as amino acids, carnitine, fatty acids, organic acids, bile acids, nucleotides, and carbohydrates, change continuously in the period after ischemia-reperfusion (24 h and 72 h), indicating abnormalities in various metabolic pathways caused by IRI-AKI.
The amino acid metabolism is inextricably associated with AKI. Decreased concentrations of valine, aspartate, and serine were observed in the renal tissues of IRI-AKI rats and corresponded to significant changes in metabolic pathways, such as the valine, leucine, and isoleucine biosynthesis pathways; phenylalanine metabolism pathway; and glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism pathways. These results are consistent with those of previous studies of metabolic changes in sepsis and sepsis-induced AKI models where increased amino acid excretion was identified as a potential marker of renal dysfunction
42
. Decreased concentrations of glutamine were also observed and corresponded to significant changes in the alanine, aspartate, and glutamate metabolic pathways. Studies have shown that glutamine prevents AKI by regulating oxidative stress and apoptosis in renal tubular epithelial cells
43
. Thus, we speculated that sustained reductions in glutamine concentration during the progression of IRI-AKI slowed the repair of kidney damage and continued to worsen kidney lesions.
Previous studies have indicated that during AKI, mitochondrial structural and functional abnormalities in renal tubular cells frequently inhibit fatty acid β-oxidation, thereby leading to the accumulation of excessive fatty acids within the kidneys
44
. As expected, our metabolomic analysis data revealed that renal tissue exhibited the accumulation of fatty acids, including adrenic acid, arachidonic acid, dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid, and 2-hydroxy-3-methylbutyric acid during IRI-AKI progression. Impaired FAO and mitochondrial dysfunction lead to ATP depletion and lipid toxicity, causing renal tubule damage, inflammation and subsequent fibrotic processes
23
,
44
. Therefore, impaired FAO acts as an early initiating factor for AKI, and fatty acids can be used as biomarkers for early monitoring of IRI-AKI. Carnitine plays a crucial role in the oxidation of fatty and branched-chain amino acids. Fatty acids can provide energy to the mitochondria in the form of acylcarnitine by binding to carnitine
45
. In our study, the levels of the most carnitine metabolites were decreased during IRI-AKI, suggesting impaired FAO and compromised energy production. This finding supports the possibility of renal tissue necrosis in the context of IRI-AKI, which aligns with the findings of previous studies
46
–
48
. Modulating the metabolic enzymes involved in FAO could be a novel early intervention strategy for IRI-AKI.
Abnormal bile acid metabolism can lead to renal failure. Bile acids are activators of a series of receptors, including the farnesoid X receptor, G-protein-coupled bile acid receptor, pregnane X receptor, vitamin D3 receptor, and constitutive androstane receptor, which regulate the physiological metabolic state of the body
49
. Our study demonstrated that the concentrations of taurodeoxycholic, glycocholic, glycodeoxycholic, and cholic acids were decreased during IRI-AKI. We speculated that the decreased expressions of bile acids during IRI-AKI development may affect their function as endogenous ligands
50
.
We observed renal injury progressively worsened during reperfusion, as confirmed by renal tissue H&E staining, TUNEL and electron microscopy, as well as serum indicators of renal function. Notably, 6 DEMs, including one amino acid and five organic acids, were upregulated in IRI-AKI 72 h group compared to IRI-AKI 24 h. In previous studies, these metabolites have been classified as neurotoxins, metabotoxins, or acidogens. Neurotoxins can damage nerve cells and neural tissues and are associated with AKI-associated delirium
51
. Acidogens are acidic compounds that can induce acidosis and have multiple adverse effects on various organ systems
52
. Metabotoxins are endogenous metabolites that cause adverse health effects at chronically high levels
53
. This study indicates that neurotoxin accumulation, systemic metabolic acidosis, and impaired amino acid excretion occur during the progression of IRIAKI
54
. However, the specific mechanisms involving these DEMs that operate during the progression of IRI-AKI require further investigation.
Transcriptomics revealed that DEGs were primarily involved in amino acid, lipid and fatty acid metabolism. These findings suggest disordered amino acid and fatty acid metabolism during the stages of IRI-AKI, which is consistent with previous reports
38
,
39
. HAVCR1, also known as kidney injury molecule-1 (KIM-1), consistently exhibited a negative correlation with the metabolites 2-hydroxyglutaric acid, gluconolactone, and methylmalonylcarnitine throughout IRI-AKI (Fig.
5
). In transcriptome analyses, the HAVCR1 gene was upregulated in the IRI-AKI 24 h and IRI-AKI 72 h groups. Although HAVCR1 is a well-validated marker of tubular injury
55
, to date, no studies have demonstrated a correlation between HAVCR1 and downstream metabolites. Our findings provide a direction for identifying downstream metabolic targets of HAVCR1. We hypothesized that HAVCR1 upregulation could lead to dysregulation in glucose, amino acid, and carnitine metabolism. Additionally, analyses in this study identified downregulation of aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) during the IRI-AKI process. Previous studies indicate that ALDH2 deficiency leads to increased reactive oxygen species production and oxidative damage
54
. ALDH2 has also been implicated in the regulation of autophagy and improvement of IRI in patients with kidney injury
56
, consistent with previous studies. Additionally, we observed that ALDH2, as a potential biological marker for IRI-AKI, was enriched in 9 and 11 metabolic pathways in the 24 h and 72 h groups, respectively (Table
S5
). These findings suggest the potential of ALDH2 as a therapeutic target for IRI-AKI. By integrating metabolomics and transcriptomics, we found valine biosynthesis, leucine biosynthesis, and isoleucine biosynthesis plays key roles in IRI-AKI development. These results provide insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying IRI-AKI and may have implications for potential therapeutic interventions.
Overall, we combined metabolomics and transcriptomics to investigate the changes and mechanisms in the progression of IRI-AKI, providing comprehensive metabolic and transcriptional profiles after kidney ischemia-reperfusion. Second, by performing the integrated analysis, we identified pathways that were commonly enriched at the metabolic and genetic levels, such as those involving the valine, leucine, and isoleucine pathways. It has been reported that the metabolism of BCAAs (branched-chain amino acids) after ingestion is initially catalyzed by branched-chain amino acid transaminases 1/2 (BCAT1/2), leading to the production of branched-chain keto acids (BCKA)
57
. These BCKA subsequently metabolized within the mitochondria to generate metabolites such as acetyl-CoA
57
. Our study also observed abnormal expression of BCAT1 and alpha-ketoisovaleric acid, which confirms the biological link from genetic abnormalities to metabolic disturbances (Fig.
6
, Figure
S2
, Table
S4
). Finally, we found genes and metabolites that have not been previously implicated in IRI-AKI development and discussed their potential as therapeutic targets, thereby providing novel insights for future research. This study also had some limitations. First, we selected only two early time points of reperfusion and analyzed a limited number of samples. Second, during this study, we primarily focused on metabolomics and transcriptomics and excluded other omics approaches, such as proteomics and single-cell transcriptomics. Third, our study used rat models. Although we identified potential therapeutic targets, these findings may not be applicable to humans. Notably, this study focused on the enrichment of DEGs and DEMs in transcriptomes and metabolomes, as well as their associated pathways. Further biological validation of these findings should be conducted in future studies. Nonetheless, this study provides new theoretical evidence and suggests molecular targets, such as HAVCR1 and ALDH2, as potential therapeutic interventions for IRI-AKI.
Conclusion
The comprehensive integration of metabolomics and transcriptomics in our study elucidated the intricate molecular landscape of IRI-AKI progression. These novel findings highlighted key metabolic and transcriptional pathways, identified potential therapeutic targets. Our research emphasized the significance of multiomics approaches to deciphering the complex pathophysiology of IRI-AKI, thereby providing new insights for targeted interventions and offering the potential to discover drugs for AKI management.
